ops.title: Automating with Zapier — Apps, AI Actions & SaaS Connections
Why Zapier at all — the dependency argument

ops.markdown:
The class opened on the fair challenge: why learn Zapier when n8n already did everything? The answer was not asserted, it was demonstrated.

**The exhibit.** A real n8n canvas of his own — schedule, GitHub push history, trending repos, filters, README fetch, four LLM chains, merge, email, plus side branches writing files back to GitHub. The class was asked to explain it. Nobody could, end to end, with ten minutes to try.

> "This flow is best understood by who created it."

The canvas is not broken and not badly built. It is unreadable by anyone else, and that turns out to be a property with consequences.

### Wanderline's three complaints

1. **It works, but it is not beginner-friendly** — "this is what keeps their Saturday and Sunday occupied." The people who live with it pay in weekends.
2. **Ownership is limited to one person.** Keep this precise: you *can* export an n8n workflow — three-dot menu gives JSON, or box-select the canvas and copy, because "all these nodes are nothing but configurations." The **artefact** is portable. What is not is that a published workflow on one account is visible and editable only by that account. Running it and owning it are different things.
3. **If that person goes, no one wants to touch it.**

**What the third one costs.** His own 2018 Excel-aggregation script, written by someone who left. `git blame` showed the lines untouched from 2018 until a 2024 migration forced the issue — because "it was vulnerable to breaking down if you make a lot of changes." Six years of nobody touching working code, not because it was wrong but because understanding it cost more than leaving it alone.

A student named it: **creating dependency.**

Note that none of the three complaints is technical. They are about who can read it, who can edit it, and who dares change it. Day 12 asked whether work suits a machine; this asks the question after it — **once built, who can live with it?**

### Zapier's structural answer

**A Zap has exactly one trigger.** n8n lets you put three, four, ten triggers and several independent workflows on one canvas. Zapier does not. One trigger, then actions, top to bottom.

Read that as a declined feature rather than a missing one. The constraint is what buys readability: one entry point and one direction means "what starts this and what happens next" has an answer you can read off the screen. The exhibit had no such answer. The trade is expressiveness for maintainability, and whether it is a good trade is what the comparison returns to.

Side note on knowledge transfer: KT videos plus `.md` files explaining the code, "so you can use that when you're using AI to make code changes." Nobody watches the videos later — but he has had to.

ops.title: Action vs task, and what it costs

ops.markdown:
**The cricket bat.** Swinging a bat in the air is an **action** — the capability exists, the motion happened. Hitting a ball that someone actually bowled is a **task**: "that is what has real tangible effect… you hit the ball and you get runs."

Translated: a *Send message* step sitting in a Zap is an action. The moment it actually sends, that is a task. A Zap that sends an email, then a chat message, then an SMS is **three tasks per run**.

This is the most consequential definition in the lecture, because it is the billing unit. Two things follow immediately:

- **The bill scales with steps × runs**, not with how many Zaps you own. Ten Zaps that never fire cost nothing; one Zap with five steps firing hourly is expensive.
- **A step that runs and achieves nothing still costs you.** Nothing about a wasted task looks different from a useful one on the invoice.

That second point is why Filter is taught as a shield rather than as a gate, and it is the whole of the filter-placement quiz.

ops.title: Zap 1 — two steps, one published Zap

ops.label: Google Sheets — New or Updated Spreadsheet Row
ops.detail:
Sheet "Wanderline Zapier" — columns name, email, trek, summary of the request, status. **Trigger column = status**: "if the status changes, I should get an update." That choice is what causes the flaw at the end of this build.

The card says **polling**. Zapier's Sheets trigger polls roughly every two minutes, and the interval is not yours to set — Zapier decides it.

Account setup, folded in from the walkthrough: 14-day trial then a monthly subscription; **no self-hosting at all** — "Zapier does not have a local open source server", which is a comparison row arriving early, and means the privacy argument for running locally has no Zapier answer. The landing page pushes an AI copilot that builds a Zap from a sentence: "Don't use it. You'll be doing it from scratch because that's what we're trying for." It does work — the manual build was to show how.

On the Google consent screen, which asks for a lot: give the permissions freely, because the review burden sits on the vendor. Getting a Drive scope approved for his own product took months of back-and-forth. That is reassurance about vendors who have been through that review, not about consent screens in general.

ops.label: Google Chat — Create a message
ops.detail:
Chat room *Wanderline Zappy*; title "Received a new request"; message text built from the trigger's fields with the **+** picker — name, trek, summary. The picker is Zapier's equivalent of n8n's drag-and-drop.

**Enhanced field mapping**: on, the picker shows column letters (A, B, C); turn it **off** to see column names. Worth turning off — a mapping written in letters is unreadable six months later.

Test step, then **Publish** as "Wanderline Zappy Chat Automation". He bumped the version on every publish, reaching 4.4 by Zap 3, with the aside that "usually you would not want to increase the version count that much".

ops.label: The flaw: any change to the trigger column sends a message
ops.detail:
A student asked him to flip the status new → reviewed → new. Each change produced a new chat message. "It does not care it's new, it does not care it's reviewed, it just sends a message. Can we agree that's wrong?"

The Zap is not broken. "Notify when the status column changes" is exactly what was asked for and exactly what is wrong — the spec was incomplete, and only running it against a real edit showed that. This is what Zap 2 fixes.

cells.c-cost: Up to about 2 minutes. A poll is scheduled, not continuous — "it closes its eyes for two minutes, then opens them and sees what's on the sheet." An edit landing just after a poll waits for the next one

cells.c-stage: The run sitting in a queue

cells.c-cost: Worst case 10–12 minutes; ideal case under two. "It usually takes about 10 minutes to reach your chat box"
Not by setting the interval — Zapier controls that, not you. Multiple new rows caught in one poll each trigger their own run

cells.c-stage: When the lag is a business problem
cells.c-cost: "You might not even want to use Google Sheets" — connect a form trigger directly instead. "It's a Google Sheet issue, not a Zapier issue": evaluate the suitability of the **node**, not the tool

When something takes longer than expected, decompose the latency into its stages before calling it a fault. None of these stages is an error and none is retryable — which is exactly why a slow run looks like a broken one

ops.markdown:
Traps collected as they came up across the lecture.

**Google Chat setup happens outside Zapier, in three steps.** At chat.google.com: install the Zapier app from *Find apps*; create a space (this is where you manage **members** — whoever should receive the automated messages); **then add the Zapier app to that space**.

**Step three is the one that gets missed**, and it did, live. The Zap's chat-room dropdown showed only an old space and refreshing did nothing; several minutes later a student spotted that the new space had not allowed apps. Note the shape of this bug — **the thing you are configuring is not missing, it is not permitted to be visible.** An empty dropdown reads as "not created yet" and actually meant "created, not authorised." No error, no message, just absence.

**A fast demo can be an accident.** The first row he added produced a message almost instantly — because he had copy-pasted it and a poll caught it mid-edit. That is not the normal experience, and he corrected it on the spot. A happy path you cannot reproduce is worse than a slow one you understand.

ops.label: Sheets trigger — unchanged from Zap 1
ops.detail: One node inserted, nothing else touched. This is the same increment discipline the n8n lecture ran on: build the minimum, run it against reality, fix what reality shows.

ops.label: Filter: only continue if status exactly matches "new"
ops.detail:
Inserted between the trigger and the chat step, which fixes the flaw Zap 1 exposed — the trigger fires on any change to the status column, so new → reviewed → new sent a message each time.

**The condition is case-sensitive.** `New` does not match `new`. That is a landmine in a spreadsheet, where a human types the status column by hand: one capitalised entry and the Zap skips a row that should have gone through. And it fails silently, because a filtered run is not an error and nothing flags it.

Zapier lays the canvas out itself — "you don't have to drag nodes, realign them; it is simpler than n8n in that sense." That falls straight out of the one-trigger, top-to-bottom constraint: when there is only one possible shape, the tool can draw it for you.

ops.label: Google Chat — create a message
ops.detail: Live test: the existing rows were set to *reviewed*, then two rows added — one *new* (a Kashmir trek booking) and one *reviewed* (a trek in Delhi, "which is not possible"). Only the *new* one reached chat.

ops.label: Run stops here
ops.detail: Not a failure and not a non-event. The run happened, the condition was evaluated, and it stopped deliberately — which Zap History records as its own status.

ops.markdown:
> "I could very well be lying to you."

**Why the demo does not prove the claim.** A message arriving in chat proves one row went through. It proves nothing about the other. Absence of a message is equally consistent with the filter working, the Zap being off, the poll not having run yet, and a delivery failure. **You cannot verify a negative from the destination.**

**What the history shows.** Home → Zap History, two runs at the same minute:

| Run | Status | What it says |
|---|---|---|
| Kashmir row | **Success** | "sent one new Create to Google Chat" |
| Delhi row | **Filtered** | "The filter successfully stopped your run. Did not attempt to send" |

**Filtered is a distinct status** — a deliberate stop, not a failure and not a non-event. Every run shows the data at each step, so you can see what the filter actually tested against. That sentence is the proof the destination could never give you: it is a statement, not an inference.

**Two loose ends.**

- **Exporting history** — not obvious from the UI; "there should be some way of directly connecting to this through API calls." Left unresolved, and he said so.
- **Auto Replay**, in the history sidebar, retries a failed run automatically for API blips. It is **paid** — the retry mechanism "comes with the premium version, not the free one."

Hold that second one for the comparison. n8n's Retry On Fail is a free checkbox in node settings on a tool you can self-host. Same capability, different commercial position — "does it retry" and "what does retrying cost you" are separate questions.

cells.c-why: "Your polling is not paid for… simply because this does not have a tangible output." How many times it opens its eyes does not matter
Sheet → LLM → email is two tasks per run, not one — and the API call is billed separately by whoever serves the model. Two meters on one step
"Anything that is doing something tangible outside Zapier is a task." Work inside the platform is free; anything that reaches out is billed
Not hours, not unlimited use. The allowance figure was given two ways in the lecture and is not recorded here

A few hundred messages a month runs smoothly on the paid plan. Thousands: "Zapier becomes expensive after a certain point" and you trade its connectivity for cost. Beyond that it is still fine if the company can afford it — but at that scale you are building your own product, not sending chat messages from Zapier

ops.title: Filter placement — the same steps, two orders

ops.label: Filter first — the AI is called on 30% of rows
Filter last — the AI is called on every row
Filter — stops about 70% of rows
ops.detail: Free. Its entire economic function is the steps it prevents.

ops.label: AI step — 1 task, on the survivors only
AI step — 1 task, on every row
ops.detail: "AI is being called every time… we are getting the summary and we are not doing anything with the summary." Seventy per cent of that spend is thrown away one step later.

ops.label: Filter — moved here "so the AI can help decide"
ops.detail: The reasoning behind the move is not stupid — sometimes you genuinely need the model's output to make the decision. The question is not whether it is sensible but what it costs, and those come apart.

ops.label: Send — 1 task
ops.detail:
Quiz answer: task usage **goes up substantially**.

A student read the explanation as "filters lower in the stack are evaluated more efficiently" — which sounds right if you are thinking of query optimisers or short-circuit evaluation. There is no optimiser here: the steps run in the order you wrote them, every time, and each one bills. His redraw: **"the lower the filter goes, the higher the cost goes."**

The rule: **put filters before tasks** — and specifically, immediately before the most expensive step the filter can legitimately guard.

ops.label: Zap B — release on a schedule. Two tasks
Sheets trigger
ops.detail: Free.

ops.label: Filter
ops.detail: Free.

ops.label: Digest — append
ops.detail: His reading of Zapier's help text, looked up live during the break and never confirmed: the built-in tools — Filter, Paths, Formatter, Digest — do not charge for **grouping** data; **releasing** the digest is what costs a task. Treat the billing rule as unverified and check it before pricing anything on it. The pattern itself stands either way.

ops.label: Schedule trigger — hourly, say
ops.detail: **This is the dial that sets the bill.** Hourly, four-hourly and daily are three very different monthly totals from an identical pair of Zaps.

ops.label: Send the email · 1 task
ops.detail:
Two tasks per release regardless of how many rows accumulated — "if you have 100 requests within an hour, you get it in two tasks only."

**What this actually does: it decouples cost from volume.** Without the digest, cost scales with rows. With it, cost scales with release frequency — a number you choose rather than one the business hands you. A variable cost has been converted into a fixed one.

**The trade, stated plainly:** delivery is hourly, not immediate. You were already accepting minutes of latency from polling; up to an hour is a different order of delay, and whether that is acceptable is a business question rather than a technical one.

**One correction.** His monthly sizing from here was about half the real figure — two tasks an hour is 48 a day, not 24 — which makes an hourly digest look more affordable than it is, possibly over the allowance he was describing it as fitting under. The pattern's logic is untouched; the sizing is not.

ops.label: Sheets trigger
ops.detail: Free.

ops.label: Filter — status is new
ops.detail: Free. Unchanged from Zap 2.

ops.label: Groq — send a prompt, one word back · 1 task
ops.detail:
App Groq ("not Elon Musk's Grok"), credentials an API key, event *Send a prompt*. Model GPT-OSS-20B — he glanced at the 120B option and took the smaller one.

The system prompt as typed, typo and all: *"Below is a request received from a client inquiring at a travel agency. <summary from the trigger>. I want you to return a single-word response suggesting whether the request is for booking, spam, or an FAQ. Based on your response we'll send it to the booking team, the FAQ team, or trash the message."*

It names the three classes, demands **a single-word response**, and tells the model what the answer will be used for. The one-word demand is what makes the path rules safe.

**The run.** Three rows: a Shimla treks question → FAQ, message arrived. "This is such a wasteful application" → classified **FAQ, not spam** — his verdict, **"that's a bad prompt from my side."** Same attribution as the n8n build: when an unambiguous input is read wrong, suspect the specification first. And a Shimla stay booking → booking, urgent message.

Zap History first showed the last two as *Filtered*, because a poll caught them before *new* had been typed in the status column; the next poll picked them up. Correctly filtered on data that was correct at that moment.

ops.label: Paths — split is free
ops.detail:
Adding a Paths step warns that everything after it moves into the first path.

**Paths double as a blocker.** There is no spam filter in this build: the absence of a matching path is the shield. That is a whitelist rather than a blacklist, and it fails in the safe direction — an unexpected output does nothing rather than something wrong.

ops.label: Path A — Chat: "New booking request, urgent action needed" · 1 task
ops.detail: Rule: *custom* — the Groq output's content (Text) **exactly matches** `booking`. Message carries name, trek and summary.

ops.label: Path B — Chat: "New FAQ request, not urgent" · 1 task
ops.detail: Rule: content exactly matches `FAQ`. Message carries the summary.

ops.label: No path matches — it goes nowhere
ops.detail:
"If it responds with spam… paths will block it. That's also a way of blocking your requests."

**Spam still costs one task** — the Groq call. The classification has to happen before you can know it is spam, so you cannot filter on a judgement you have not made yet. That is the irreducible floor, and it is why filtering before the AI step only works when the condition is something you already know.

ops.markdown:
**The quiz.** A reply contains both BOOKING and CONTENT; Path A matches on BOOKING, Path B on CONTENT. What runs?

**Both paths run in full, and it costs tasks for all three actions.**

> "Path is not like a conditional statement. Both of them are true, go for both of them."

**Why it catches people.** `if / else if` trains you to expect the first match to win. Paths are not that. They are **independent conditions**, each evaluated on its own, and every one that is true executes its whole branch.

**Both sides, as he gave them:**

- **Good for control** — you can genuinely want two things to happen.
- **Scary for cost** — unconfigured, "your cost is going to double whatever you had predicted."
- **Nesting compounds it** — "two tasks on the top and two tasks at the bottom… it would increase your cost massively."

**Against filter placement.** That was about steps you *avoid*. This is about steps you did not know you were **authorising** — and it multiplies rather than adds.

Two properties, working together, are what keep this build off two paths at once:

1. **The system prompt demands one word.**
2. **The path rules use *exactly matches*, not *contains*.**

**Follow it through.** A request that is both a booking and a question still yields one word — probably `booking`, from the opening clause. And if the model ever returned `"booking FAQ"`, that string equals neither rule, so it goes down **no path** rather than both.

> "My system prompt ensures that I do not go in two paths."

**Why this is properly designed rather than lucky.** *Contains* would match both rules on `"booking FAQ"` and fire both branches. *Exactly matches* **fails closed** — an unexpected output drops out of the flow instead of triggering everything. The prompt narrows what can be produced; the match rule ensures anything outside that narrow set does nothing.

**This is the n8n homework arriving from the other direction.** There, a tag appended to prose could not be tested safely and the fix was to emit a field and branch on it. Here the whole output *is* the value and the comparison is exact. Same principle — make the branch read something unambiguous — implemented at the prompt rather than in the output format.

cells.c-what: A Filter stopped it on purpose. Not a failure and not a non-event — the run happened and the stop was deliberate
Queued, not run. Usually out of tasks; also a paused Zap, or one you held yourself
A step threw. Debug by clicking into the run
cells.c-alert: Yes — Zapier emails the Zap's owner

cells.c-what: Halted before finishing, often a missing required field
cells.c-alert: Rare in production — "usually happens during configuration"

cells.c-what: Error alerts you. Held does not
cells.c-alert: The failure mode most likely on a metered plan — quietly exhausting the allowance mid-month — is precisely the one that says nothing

ops.markdown:
**The illustration.** A 1,000-task credit, 900 used, and 120 more requests arrive. Around 200 runs sit as **Held**.

> "My workflow will not fail. My workflow will get stuck."

Nothing errors. Nothing emails.

**The quiz.** Runs on Thursday all Held, none since, no error emails — most likely cause? **The account ran out of tasks.** Runs queue as Held, nothing errors, so no alert is sent.

The eliminations are as useful as the answer:

- **A disconnected credential gives Error, not Held** — a different status, and it would have emailed you. The presence of Held and the absence of email both point away from it.
- **Editing the sheet does not stop polling.** He hedged this one — "could potentially cause it to stop maybe, but not held" — so treat the first half as unsettled. What the question turns on is that it is not what Held means, and that part is solid.
- **Replay does not throttle.**

**A Zap is never inactive.** Asked whether inactive means stopped: no — it polls and waits. "If nothing is happening, nothing is happening, but the workflow will continue running." **Quiet and stopped are different states.**

Which gives the diagnostic pair: **an empty history and a Held history mean different things, and neither is an error.** One says nothing ever started. The other says everything started and nothing was allowed to proceed.

**The through-line.** This is the third form of one shape across the automation block — a built-but-unpublished workflow that never triggers, an execution history with nothing in it, and now runs sitting Held. In all three the system behaves correctly, reports nothing, and produces no output. **The absence of an error is not evidence of health**, and on a metered platform the thing to monitor is the meter, not the error channel.

A lightweight database inside Zapier — rows, typed columns. And the part the printed panel says matters: **it can be a trigger too.** A new or updated record starts another Zap, "closing a loop the leads spreadsheet never could: **your automation now owns its own data instead of borrowing someone's file.**"

Every build so far has been reading and writing somebody else's file — a Google Sheet that happens to be reachable. Tables makes the data part of the automation rather than a dependency it reaches out to.

**The availability argument**, which came out of a student saying "less connections": with Google Sheets there are **two players**, Zapier and Google, so the Sheets API, the network or Google itself can fail — rarely, but the surface exists. Tables live "in the same cloud structure" as the Zaps, so "even if the outer-world connection was broken, the inner connection will not break."

**The boundary he was careful about.** This is **not** a reason to move everything off Drive. It is a reason to use Tables where reliability and speed matter.

That is a proportionate claim and worth keeping as one. A failure surface existing is not by itself a reason to remove a dependency — a shared sheet that humans edit is doing a job a table cannot do, which is being a file people can open. The question is per-integration: does *this* dependency carry risk worth removing? Same shape as "it's a Google Sheet issue, not a Zapier issue" — evaluate the node.

It also lands on the cost boundary: Tables is inside the platform, and work inside the platform is the free side of the line.

**Left as self-study** — create a table from the left nav, then add, read and delete rows from a Zap. One of the two things set as homework.

ops.title: Zapier or n8n — the honest comparison

cells.c-zap: A numbered list, top to bottom — "on the prettiness scale, Zapier wins"
cells.c-n8n: A canvas with branches going anywhere

cells.c-dim: Who can maintain it — the headline
cells.c-zap: Anyone in the business. "Kabir, you're fired, I'll take care of this"
cells.c-n8n: Whoever built it. "Kabir builds a dependency; the company is never firing Kabir. If you want job security, go for n8n" — the joke names the incentive honestly: what is bad for the business is good for the person who owns the flow

cells.c-zap: Point at a pill. No syntax to learn
cells.c-n8n: Expressions and a JSON item model — more power, a real learning curve

cells.c-zap: Thousands — the long tail is the point; the obscure SaaS your client uses is probably there
cells.c-n8n: Fewer pre-built, but the HTTP node reaches anything — "not necessarily far behind, but more complicated"

cells.c-zap: Per task. Predictable, and scales up with volume. Worse in absolute terms, better in legibility — you can forecast it, expense it and hand it to someone else
cells.c-n8n: Free if self-hosted — paid in server, upgrades and your own time. **"The cost of n8n is your life; the cost of Zapier is the actual cost"**

cells.c-zap: Through Zapier's servers — "if you want to preserve the data, Zapier is not the best option". No self-hosting exists
cells.c-n8n: Wherever you host it, including entirely inside your own network

cells.c-zap: Gets expensive fast — per-task pricing scales linearly with runs
cells.c-n8n: Barely notices — "n8n is the winner here very clearly"
Native and expected — "bring your coding hat"

cells.c-dim: Retrying a failed run — not on the panel
cells.c-zap: Auto Replay — a paid tier; "comes with the premium version, not the free one"
cells.c-n8n: Retry On Fail — a free checkbox in node settings. This row is assembled from the two lectures, not printed on the comparison panel: same capability, different commercial position

ops.markdown:
**What "volume" means in the cost row.** Rows → runs → tasks. **1,000 rows = 1,000 chats = 1,000 tasks.** The size of each row's data is not what is billed.

A thousand one-line rows costs the same as a thousand paragraph-long ones. Worth holding because the cloud-pricing intuition — you pay by the amount of data — points the wrong way here. What is metered is how many times something happens.

**Per task, Zapier sets no data-size limit.** Google Chat, though, has a message-length cap — so for a big payload, write it to a sheet instead of posting it. And the honest close: "some things like a high volume might require a different tool."

**Limits live in the integrations.** That is the third time this lecture made the same move:

- the polling interval belongs to the **Sheets** trigger,
- the message cap belongs to **Google Chat**,
- and Zapier owns neither.

When something constrains a flow, ask which integration the constraint lives in before blaming the platform.

**RAG** is possible in both tools — "provide documentation to AI agents."

*This note is a reading of the two lectures side by side. Neither instructor put it this way.*

**The two rules.** The workflow-automation lecture landed on: use the flexible tool by default — n8n — unless a connector you need is missing, in which case use Zapier. This panel's headline is **maintainability**, and it points the other way.

**They answer different questions.** Day 12 compared *capability* — what each tool can express, and what stops you. This comparison is about *consequences* — what happens to the flow after it is built, when someone else owns it.

**So: the Day 12 rule optimises for the build. The Day 14 headline optimises for the life of the thing afterwards.**

Which should decide depends on whether the automation is yours to keep:

- **A personal pipeline** that only you will ever touch has no dependency problem. Capability wins, and the Day 12 rule stands.
- **Anything handed to a business** has one. Then maintainability outranks the connector question.

The reason for the ordering: **a missing connector is a problem you find on day one. An unmaintainable flow is a problem you find in year three** — after its author has left, when nobody dares change it.

One row can override both: where the data must not leave your own network, there is no Zapier answer at all, whatever the rest of the table says.
